extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers, students, and professional mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: Expositing what mathematics is, how it is practiced, taught, and transmitted — aimed at both general readers and professionals. The text surveys definitions, methodology (proof), tools, community norms, and philosophical questions about mathematical existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naive definition: mathematics as the science of quantity and space
rubrics_metrics.description: “NAIVE DEFINITION, adequate for the dictionary and for an initial understanding, is that mathematics is the science of quantity and space.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanded phrasing in text: add that mathematics also deals with the symbolism relating to quantity and to space. The authors note this definition has historical basis but should be modified to reflect growth of the subject over centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as a deductive science (proof-centered methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclidean geometry is presented “as a deductive science... beginning with a number of elementary ideas which are assumed to be self-evident, and on the basis of a few definite rules of mathematical and logical manipulation... builds up a fabric of deductions of increasing complexity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof (the deductive process) is highlighted as the methodological core taught in geometry and as the model for formalized deductive systems; studying geometry is held to provide basic training in logical thinking and proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peirce's formulation: mathematics as the science of making necessary conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: C. S. Peirce: “'mathematics is the science of making necessary conclusions.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes the structural pattern assumption→deduction→conclusion and implies mathematics could be about anything that fits that pattern; the text gives an illustrative (tongue-in-cheek) example comparing detection to mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of proof vs discovery (proof as verification rather than the locus of invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion from the Introduction: “The fact is... my wonderment... is equal to... doing mathematics. ... Theorems are not to mathematics what successful courses are to a meal. ... proof, far from being the core of discovery, is more often than not a way of making sure that our minds are not playing tricks.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides readers to view mathematical discovery as involving guesswork, analogy, and intuition; proof often arrives after conjecture to secure results rather than being the initial creative act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility with scientific standards (avoid oversimplification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gian-Carlo Rota's introduction: “Making mathematics accessible to the educated layman, while keeping high scientific standards, has always been considered a treacherous navigation between the Scylla of professional contempt and the Charybdis of public misunderstanding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors aim to describe mathematics candidly for nonprofessionals but insist on preserving scientific rigor and avoiding harmful oversimplification; balance clarity for lay readers with fidelity to technical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools necessary for doing mathematics: writing/recording and duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is by no means fair to say that mathematics is done totally in the head... to do mathematics one must have, at the very least, instruments of writing or recording and of duplication. Before the invention of printing, there were 'scribe factories' for the wholesale replication of documents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While thought-experiments are important, the text emphasizes practical auxiliaries (writing implements, recording media, printing) as indispensable for development, preservation, and transmission of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler-and-compass as foundational tools in Euclidean geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ruler and compass are built into the axioms at the foundation of Euclidean geometry. Euclidean geometry can be defined as the science of ruler-and-compass constructions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides a methodological standard for Euclidean geometry: constructions and allowable operations are part of the formal system and hence part of what counts as acceptable practice in that subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of definitions: definitions of mathematics change with perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: “The definition of mathematics changes. Each generation and each thoughtful mathematician within a generation formulates a definition according to his lights.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should expect and accept that 'what mathematics is' is mutable; the book proceeds to examine alternate formulations rather than asserting a single final definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where mathematics 'exists' is a philosophical question (mind, texts, machines, artifacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions raised: mathematics exists on the printed page, in people's minds, on taped lectures, in computer memories and printed circuits, in machines, perhaps even in biological forms; philosophers debate whether real mathematics exists eternally and independently of actualizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No prescriptive resolution is offered here, but the passage frames a criterion: accounts of mathematics should address its modes of existence (mental, social, physical, platonic) and the implications of each view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community norms: openness, publication, and meetings as standards of mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mathematics of today is unified. It is worked and transmitted in full and open knowledge. There is a vast international network of publications; there are national and international open meetings and exchanges of scholars and students.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for healthy mathematical practice: open dissemination, peer exchange, and broad publication are indicators of a functioning mathematical community; secrecy is anomalous except for wartime/cryptography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional evaluation: advancement depends on peer judgment within the field
rubrics_metrics.description: “My advancement was dependent on my research and publication in my field... there were important rewards for mastering the outlook and ways of thought shared by those whose training was similar to mine. Their judgment would decide the value of what I did.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets a standard for assessing mathematical work: peers trained in the same subfield are the primary evaluators; alignment with disciplinary norms and publication record are key to professional recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as widespread human activity (not limited to professionals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' claim: “Mathematics has been a human activity for thousands of years. To some small extent, everybody is a mathematician and does mathematics consciously. To buy at the market, to measure a strip of wallpaper or to decorate a ceramic pot with a regular pattern is doing mathematics.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides pedagogical and social perspectives: policies and educational materials should recognize mathematical activity at many levels and contexts, and not confine 'mathematics' to formal professional practice.
